# TypeScript API

Live values and `ssr:bind` work without any TypeScript. Write some to call the page's calls, to show a
validation message, to react to connection loss, or to drive a custom widget.

## The generated client

Every route with live values or page calls gets a generated `__ssr_gen__.ts` next to its `index.html`:

```typescript
// Code generated by github.com/sergei-svistunov/go-ssr. DO NOT EDIT.
import { createSsrClient } from 'gossr-runtime';
import 'gossr-runtime/ssr-block.css';

export interface LastSeenOut {
  lastSeen: string;
  at: string;
}

export type ReadVars = {
  displayName: string;
  lastSeen: string;
}

export type WriteVars = {
  displayName: string;
}

export type Calls = {
  refreshLastSeen: { in: Record<string, never>; out: LastSeenOut };
}

export const ssr = createSsrClient<ReadVars, WriteVars, Calls>({ … });
```

- `ReadVars` lists every reactive variable of the route. Each is a `string`: the markup the server rendered for
  the variable's plain `{{ name }}` site, not the Go value.
- `WriteVars` lists the `client-writable` variables, each with its Go type mapped to TypeScript.
- `Calls` lists the route's page calls, each with its argument and result types.
- Types are mapped from the route package's declarations as `encoding/json` writes them: a struct becomes an
  interface with its JSON field names, `time.Time` a `string`, a pointer `T | null`. A type the generator cannot
  name exactly becomes `unknown`, with a warning.

The WebSocket URL, which carries the page's query string, and the route key are filled in by the generator.
The webpack plugin bundles `__ssr_gen__.ts` into the route's chunk whether or not you write an `index.ts`, so
the connection opens on every such page automatically.

## Using it

```typescript
import { ssr } from './__ssr_gen__';
```

| Call | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `ssr.get(name)` | the last markup received for the variable's plain `{{ name }}` site, or `undefined` |
| `ssr.on(name, cb)` | run `cb(markup)` when the init or a patch for that site arrives |
| `ssr.set(name, value)` | write a value to the server; only accepts `client-writable` names |
| `ssr.call(name, args)` | run a page call; resolves with its result, rejects with a `CallError` |
| `ssr.onError(cb)` | `cb(varName, message)` when the server rejects a write |
| `ssr.onConnect(cb)` | connection established or re-established |
| `ssr.onDisconnect(cb)` | `cb(code, reason)` when an established connection drops unexpectedly |
| `ssr.onConnectError(cb)` | `cb(status)` when the upgrade request is rejected; `status` is always 0, since browsers do not expose it |
| `ssr.stop()` | close the page's live connection for good, for every route on the page |

Every subscription function returns an unsubscribe function.

`get` and `on` take a variable name and give the string as received: escaped **markup**, not decoded text.
The runtime has already applied it to the DOM by the time your callback runs, so use these for side effects
rather than for rendering. Never write the string into `innerHTML` unless you mean it as markup, and never
into `textContent` if you want the text: a value `a < b` arrives as `a &lt; b`.

```typescript
const errorEl = document.getElementById('display-name-error');

ssr.onError((varName, message) => {
    if (varName === 'displayName' && errorEl) {
        errorEl.textContent = message;
    }
});

ssr.on('displayName', () => {
    if (errorEl) errorEl.textContent = '';
});
```

`ssr.set` is fire and forget, and a write made while the connection is down is dropped. The value comes back as
a normal patch once the server has validated it, so do not treat a `set` call as having taken effect until
then:

```typescript
ssr.set('displayName', 'Ada');
```

Calling `set` with a name that is not in `WriteVars`, or `call` with a name that is not in `Calls`, is a
TypeScript compile error, which is the point of the generated types.

## Page calls

```typescript
import { CallError } from 'gossr-runtime';
import { ssr } from './__ssr_gen__';

const label = document.getElementById('last-seen')!;

async function refresh(): Promise<void> {
    try {
        const out = await ssr.call('refreshLastSeen', {});
        label.textContent = out.lastSeen;
    } catch (err) {
        label.textContent = err instanceof CallError ? err.message : 'The call failed.';
    }
}
```

`CallError` carries `status` and `message`. A status the server sent comes with a message meant for the page;
status 0 means `The connection was lost.` before the answer came — the call may still have run on the server.
The runtime never retries a call. A call made while the connection is down waits for it to open; every waiting
call goes out at once, so some may get 429. See `page-calls` for every status.

## Connection state

```typescript
const banner = document.getElementById('offline')!;

ssr.onDisconnect((code, reason) => banner.hidden = false);
ssr.onConnect(() => banner.hidden = true);
ssr.onConnectError(() => location.reload());
```

- `onDisconnect` does not fire on normal navigation away from the page, on a 1000 close, or when the runtime
  closes the connection because the tab is hidden.
- Reconnection is automatic: at once after a 4000 close from a connection that was open at least 30 seconds,
  with back-off after any other unexpected close. 1000 and 1001 are final. After it succeeds the server sends
  a fresh init frame with every current value, so the page does not need reloading.
- While the tab is hidden the connection is closed; calls in flight reject with status 0. It reopens when the
  tab is shown again, and a refused upgrade then retries with back-off and rejects the calls waiting at that
  moment. A socket that opens resets the count of refusals.
- A refused upgrade — the first one, one after a drop, or the third in a row after the tab is shown again — is
  final and fires `onConnectError`; waiting calls reject with status 0 and later calls at once. The session
  may have ended: reload the page there.
- A 1008 close means a `Subscribe` refused the session or a guard refused a call; the runtime logs the
  server's reason and reconnects with back-off, and the new handshake passes the guards again or is refused.
- `ssr.stop()` ends the page's connection for good. All routes on a page share it, so `stop()` on any route's
  client stops every route: none reconnects, `set` warns and page calls reject with status 0. It fires no
  callback. The event that ended a connection reaches every route's `onDisconnect` or `onConnectError` once,
  even when an earlier handler calls `stop()`, so any route can stop the page from its handler:

```typescript
ssr.onDisconnect((code) => {
    if (code === 1008) {
        ssr.stop();
        banner.hidden = false;
    }
});
```

## Packages and configuration

```json
{
  "dependencies": { "gossr-runtime": "^0.2.0" },
  "devDependencies": { "gossr-assets-webpack-plugin": "^0.1.1" }
}
```

- **`gossr-runtime`** — the client: WebSocket handling, the shared-connection multiplexer, the DOM patcher,
  page calls and the `ssr` object. Also ships `gossr-runtime/ssr-block.css`, which the generated file imports
  so wrapper elements do not affect layout.
- **`gossr-assets-webpack-plugin`** — emits `webpack-assets.json` for the generator and copies images into the
  static output.

go-ssr 0.7.0 needs gossr-runtime 0.2.0, and gossr-runtime 0.2.0 needs go-ssr 0.7.0. Nothing checks the pairing
at run time, so upgrade both together.

`tsconfig.json` needs `"moduleResolution": "bundler"` or `"nodenext"` so the runtime's `exports` map is
honoured.

## Per-route entry points

`index.ts` and `styles.scss` next to a template are bundled into that route's chunk and loaded by
`<ssr:assets/>`. A parent route's chunk loads on every page beneath it, so shared behaviour belongs in the
layout's `index.ts` and page-specific behaviour in the page's own. They are the only place for scripts and
styles: the Content-Security-Policy blocks inline code (`security`).
